summary:
The federal Self-Determination Act (Selbstbestimmungsgesetz, SBGG) governs every step of a trans visitor's stay in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Approved by the federal cabinet in August 2023, passed by the Bundestag in April 2024 by 374 votes to 251 and in force since 1 November 2024, it lets adults over 18 change their legal first name and gender entry by self-declaration with three months' notice and no medical certification. No Mecklenburg-Vorpommern-specific trans statute, placement reform or ordinance is recorded in the sources; the federal framework applies here in full, including to short-term visitors and their documents at check-in and border or identity checks.

The partner baseline is the federal one as well: same-sex marriage with full marital and adoption rights has been available since 1 October 2017, implementing legislation having been passed on 30 June 2017. A married or registered partner travelling with a trans visitor is recognised on those terms in this Land.

Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure, and it is precisely where this Land is the flashpoint. German prisons operate under statutory separation on a binary men and women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been applied only in exceptional cases; the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony gives that reading of the prison-act provision in force in its own state as the operating rule and runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Some Länder have since amended their prison statutes to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026.

According to Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026, prison placement under the SBGG follows the person's legal gender entry unless the applicable state prison law provides otherwise. Whether the exception clauses are abstract (applied to any prisoner where individual risk outweighs interests) or drafted to target trans prisoners specifically is contested among the Länder and is now a live legislative question across the federation.

Mecklenburg-Vorpommern is the jurisdiction in which that exception was applied against the legal gender entry. On 15–17 July 2026 the Landgericht Neubrandenburg ruled that the prisoner known as the Liebich case serve her sentence in a men's prison despite a completed legal gender change; France24 and wire coverage of 16 July 2026 reported the placement as proceeding on that basis. The case drew Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia into a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, so the exposure identified here is not confined to this Land.

The same pattern is documented elsewhere in Germany and sets the expectation a trans visitor should carry into any arrest or prolonged detention. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle stated that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry was changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. After her extradition from Czechia in July 2026 she was transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman since 2025; authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility, and critics characterised the gender change as an abuse of the self-determination law. DW reported on 23 August 2023 that German prisons offer few safe spaces for trans inmates, illustrating the point with the case of climate activist Penelope Frank of Last Generation, legally recorded male, who faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted. The Berlin prison service maintains an official page in German with information and contacts for trans, inter and non-binary persons held across the city's facilities — the only facility-level support resource in the sources.

Airport and identity screening is a documented flashpoint for visitors rather than residents. In June 2025 the DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, in which officers allegedly deliberately disregarded her gender identity; she characterised the incident as a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment and gave Resident Advisor a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected facilities has been contested since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off public argument about registered trans women's access, in which trans woman Alessia Dorigo argued that claiming a trans identity on a whim is unrealistic. Tagesspiegel Queerspiegel reported on how Berlin saunas and similar venues now treat trans women after months of argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused. A visitor should expect facility operators in this Land to apply similar private or association-level criteria.

Support machinery for hostility encountered in country exists at national level. The STOP the HATE campaign site, run by the Prevention and Empowerment organisation in northern Germany, provides a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.
tangentialFactors:
The Liebich case is the pivot of an ongoing federal political process, not an isolated incident. France24 and wire coverage of 16 July 2026 recorded that the placement prompted Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia to open a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, and Verfassungsblog's 18 March 2026 analysis had already mapped the abstract-versus-trans-targeted exception clauses that the initiative would sharpen. A visitor in this Land may face a rule set that changes between arrival and any later contact with the criminal-justice system.

Comparison across the Länder shows divergence rather than a settled national position. Rhineland-Palatinate legislated expressly in its prison act, with § 17 taking effect on 1 March 2026; the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony continues to treat gender-identity placement as exceptional practice under that state's older provision; DW's 23 August 2023 reporting and the Berlin prison service's trans-specific contact page show that some administrations run dedicated procedures while others do not. Mecklenburg-Vorpommern's own prison-act text is not described in the sources, so the position here cannot be read off the examples.

Non-custodial exposure is drawn from two adjacent areas rather than from this Land. The BASHKKA complaint concerns an airport screening in another state under the federal Equal Treatment Act, which a visitor here would be equally able to invoke; the outcome of that complaint is not stated in the sources. The sauna dispute is a private-sector and association-rule matter — the Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline of January 2025 and the Tagesspiegel Queerspiegel reporting on Berlin venues — and shows that facility access after the Self-Determination Act has been governed by operator practice more than by statute.
localsOnly:
Residents and long-term trans visitors in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern hold their legal name and gender entry on the federal SBGG route: self-declaration after three months' notice, no medical certificate, in force since 1 November 2024 and available in every Land. The 374–251 Bundestag vote of April 2024 and the cabinet approval of August 2023 are the legislative record behind that entitlement, and no separate Mecklenburg-Vorpommern trans statute is recorded.

For residents facing criminal proceedings, the operative question is how the Neubrandenburg court's July 2026 placement ruling treats their own legal gender entry, and whether the state's prison act contains an exception clause of the abstract or the trans-targeted kind. Verfassungsblog's 18 March 2026 analysis identifies that distinction as decisive and unsettled. Residents who are detained should request that their SBGG-issued documents be placed in the file at intake, as intake review was the stated mechanism in the Halle prosecutor's position on the Chemnitz placement in August 2025.

Residents are protected, as in every Land, by the federal Equal Treatment Act and by the hate-crime support apparatus described in the STOP the HATE campaign: a topic-sorted counselling finder, an LSBTIQ* crisis line for emergencies, and guidance on evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels for incidents of hostility. The Berlin prison service's page for trans, inter and non-binary detainees is the only administration-level example in the sources; no comparable Mecklenburg-Vorpommern contact point is recorded.

The sources establish the federal rule and the Neubrandenburg ruling, but not the state-level statutory basis on which the Neubrandenburg court acted.

Unresolved and not sourced: the current status of the Liebich prison placement and of the Bundesrat initiative opened by Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia to tighten the Self-Determination Act, and whether any of the resulting legislation has taken effect since 16 July 2026.

Unresolved and not sourced: any Mecklenburg-Vorpommern-specific support or reporting body for trans visitors.
